correctness.rationale: The proof partitions all PSD Gaussian covariances by variance of the second difference and by the independent regression residual second moment. The conditional pole-tail lemma gives both exact one-sided constants with Gaussian truncation controlling all other large deviations. Algebraic equivalence of zero residual with preserved geometric ratio, layer-cake moment integrals, and direct exchangeable covariance substitution complete the classification. A reproducible standalone script completed 93 assertions; the infinite-domain result is supported by the analytic proof rather than enumeration.

originality.rationale: The classical Aitken rational identity, warnings about near-zero denominators, and Cauchy-type tails for other Gaussian rational accelerators are preexisting. The asserted new fact is specifically the complete positive-semidefinite covariance classification for three noisy geometric observations and its balanced explicit one-sided tail constant, including the exact perfect-correlation boundary. Direct comparisons to deterministic Aitken/ Shanks methods, noisy fixed-data Aitken gradient estimation, heavy-tailed SGD, and earlier two-evaluation Gaussian Anderson calculations did not imply that exact statement. Precedence remains a genuine risk.
residual_risks: An uncatalogued specialist noisy-Shanks or Gaussian-ratio calculation may already state the covariance knife-edge, even under different terminology.

The 2015 Buoso–Karapiperi–Pozza Aitken generalizations were identified but the complete article was not established as read; its deterministic description suggests lower overlap risk, not proof of noncoverage.

General reciprocal-normal distribution theory could yield the pole-tail lemma as an immediate specialization; the application and covariance classification, not that generic lemma alone, supply value.

value.rationale: Aitken and Shanks transforms are used on noisy numerical observations, and choosing correlated/common random numbers is a real design decision. The result exactly distinguishes a stable Gaussian or Gaussian-polynomial output from an output without any finite first absolute moment, despite arbitrarily small noise, and quantifies the rare-event coefficient. It identifies precisely which correlation structure removes the pole. This is a motivated numerical stability diagnostic, not a gratuitous finite table or a restatement of the familiar small-denominator warning.
